channel.title: peplomer
channel.description: Research at the seam between neuroscience and machine learning. Every analogy rated, every mapping's limits stated.

item.title: What peplomer is
item.description: A reading guide to a publication that puts the brain and the machine side by side, and refuses to pretend they are the same.

item.title: The three sides: biological, computational, and the bridge
item.description: Three colours carry the whole argument. Blue is a claim about brains, red is a claim about machines, and yellow is a claim that the two line up.

item.title: How to read a correspondence
item.description: Every claim that the brain and the model line up gets one of three words, and a paragraph that says where it stops being true.

item.title: The predicting brain, in plain terms
item.description: Your brain is not waiting for the world to tell it what is out there. It is guessing, constantly, and paying attention mostly to what it got wrong.

item.title: How a language model learns, in plain terms
item.description: A language model is trained to do one narrow thing, guess the next word, billions of times, until the guessing encodes a great deal about the world.

item.title: Predictive processing and the prediction objective
item.description: The brain spends its life guessing the next signal and correcting the guess. So does a language model. The shared verb is real. The reasons behind it are not the same.

item.title: Dual-process theory, metacognition, and the reasoning trace
item.description: A page of step-by-step working looks like the slow, careful system switching on. In a language model it is the same forward pass, only longer, and the trace can lie about what happened.

item.title: Consolidation, replay, and agent memory architecture
item.description: The brain keeps a fast store and a slow one and moves experience between them while you sleep. Agent memory has the same layers, and one operation biology runs automatically that no vector store performs.

item.title: Reward prediction error, actor-critic, and the alignment of objectives
item.description: Dopamine neurons compute the temporal-difference error of reinforcement learning, confirmed in single cells. RLHF reuses that exact machinery. The strength of the algorithm hides how different the two rewards are.

item.title: Framing, anchoring, and the behavioral economics of the prompt
item.description: Prompt sensitivity looks like framing, position bias looks like the serial-position curve, and leading eval prompts look like demand characteristics. The resemblance is real and the mechanisms are not shared.
